summary: This experimental memo defines the Context Transfer Protocol, which lets authorised state about a mobile node be passed between access routers. Moving this context can reduce delay and signalling overhead during a handover.

eli5.summary: When you move to a new teacher, your old teacher passes on notes about you so you do not have to start over. This protocol does that between routers.

questions: what is the context transfer protocol
how does context transfer help handover
how does cxtp reduce handover delay
when is context transfer predictive vs reactive
subtitle: Transferring mobile node state between routers during handover.

tldr.problem: When a mobile node moves between network access routers, it must re-establish context (QoS settings, security associations, multicast memberships) from scratch, causing handover delay and signaling overhead.
tldr.mechanism: CXTP defines messages for access routers to transfer stored context about a mobile node before or after handover, reducing re-establishment time.
tldr.outcome: Context transfer reduces handover latency and signaling, though the protocol is experimental and requires IPsec security between routers.

today: RFC 4067 is an Experimental protocol, not a standard. It defines mechanisms for context transfer during mobile handovers and has served as a basis for understanding seamless mobility in IP networks, though deployment has been limited to research and experimental deployments.

sections.title: The Handover Problem
sections.content:
Context Transfer Protocol (CXTP) addresses a challenge in mobile IP networks. When a mobile node moves from one access router (pAR) to another (nAR), it must re-establish many features: Quality of Service parameters, multicast group memberships, authentication states, and other per-flow settings. This re-establishment takes time and generates signaling traffic.

CXTP lets the previous router transfer this accumulated state to the new router before the handover completes, or even during it. The result is faster handovers with less disruption to running applications.
sections.eli5: Instead of your new teacher asking you everything about your learning again, your old teacher passes along notes. The new teacher reads the notes and can help you immediately without starting over.

sections.title: How Context Transfer Works
sections.content:
CXTP operates in three scenarios. In predictive transfer, the previous router detects a handover in advance (for example, via radio signal strength), sends the mobile node a Context Transfer Activate Request (CTAR) message to the new router, and pushes context data (CTD) before the node disconnects. In reactive transfer, the handover is unexpected, and the new router requests context from the previous router on receiving the CTAR. In mobile-controlled transfer, the mobile node itself sends CTAR to both routers.

Each context type is identified by a Feature Profile Type (FPT) code registered with IANA. Context data is carried in Context Data Blocks (CDBs), which hold feature-specific parameters and use a presence vector to indicate which fields are present.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to pass notes: the old teacher mails them ahead, the new teacher calls and asks for them, or your parents give you a copy to hand over yourself.

sections.title: CXTP Messages
sections.content:
CXTP defines six message types. CTAR (Context Transfer Activate Request) is sent by the mobile node to both routers; it carries the node's IP addresses, a sequence number, and an HMAC-SHA1 authorization token computed over the requested contexts. CTAA (Activate Acknowledge) is an optional reply reporting success or failure per Feature Profile Type. CTD (Context Transfer Data) carries the actual context from the previous router to the new router, including keying material to let the new router verify the mobile node's token. CTDR (Context Transfer Data Reply) reports success or failure. CTC (Context Transfer Cancel) stops an in-progress transfer. CT-Req (Context Transfer Request) is sent by the new router to request context from the previous router.

Messages between routers use SCTP with congestion control and retransmission. Messages between mobile node and router use ICMP.
sections.eli5: Six types of notes are sent: the mobile node says 'please transfer my context', the routers send back 'got it' or 'failed', and they can ask each other for more details or cancel if needed.

sections.title: Security and Authorization
sections.content:
The protocol faces threats from masquerading attacks (a rogue node requesting transfers) and denial-of-service attacks (requesting many transfers then disappearing). Routers must authenticate and authorize both the mobile node and each other.

Between access routers, CXTP MUST be protected by IPsec ESP with non-null encryption and authentication. Routers SHOULD pre-establish IPsec Security Associations to avoid delay during handovers. Between mobile node and router, the CTAR message includes an authorization token calculated as HMAC-SHA1 over the previous address, sequence number, and requested contexts. The shared secret key is established separately and must be discarded immediately after use; the mobile node MUST establish a new key for future transfers. Routers SHOULD rate-limit CTAR messages (default: 10 per second) to limit DoS attacks.
sections.eli5: Only trusted routers can talk to each other using encrypted secret codes. The mobile node proves it is allowed to transfer by showing a special number that both the old router and the node computed the same way.

sections.title: Handover Flow Examples
sections.content:
In a predictive network-controlled handover, the previous router receives a trigger (from the mobile node or internally), sends CTD proactively, the mobile node sends CTAR to the new router, and the new router replies with CTDR.

In a reactive network-controlled handover, the new router sends CT-Req first, because it does not yet have context, then the previous router replies with CTD.

In mobile-controlled transfer, the mobile node sends CTAR to its current access router before moving, to trigger a predictive transfer, then sends CTAR to the new router, which may have already received the context or may request it from the previous router.

The protocol accommodates both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. Transfer is timed: the previous router retains context for CT_MAX_TRANSFER_TIME (200 ms default) and retransmits CTD on timeout. The mobile node retransmits CTAR if needed, starting after CT_REQUEST_RETRY (2 seconds) and giving up after CT_RETRY_MAX (15 seconds).
sections.eli5: Three examples show how the three roles (old router, new router, mobile node) exchange context at different moments: before the device moves, right as it moves, or after it has already switched routers.
